title: Once-for-All: Scalable Simultaneous Forecasting via Equilibrium State Estimation
topic: General Machine Learning->Sequential, Network, and Time Series Modeling
claim: Interacting systems evolve toward a shared equilibrium state, and each system's deviation from it defines its next change.
layout: 4 panels, left-to-right with arrows, equilibrium line plots above stacked bars
description: Four panels run left to right, linked by black arrows and labeled with time steps t0, tp, tp+q and tp+q+r. Each panel has a small line plot on top and a stacked bar chart below. The bar chart shows three systems, A, B and C. Each bar stacks three attributes in blue, green and orange. The line plot above each chart shows the equilibrium state as a red solid line with red dots. It also shows the current state as a purple dotted line with purple crosses. Blue arrows point from the current state to the equilibrium where the two differ, as in t0 and tp+q. In tp and tp+q+r the two lines coincide, so the systems are at equilibrium. A legend on the right explains the markers and the three attribute colors. The eye goes first to the colorful bars and then to the line plots.
caption: Illustration of three systems (A, B, and C) reaching equilibrium under four scenarios. Each system is characterized by the same set of three attributes. The red solid line above A, B, C in each scenario represents the corresponding equilibrium state ($\mathcal{ES}$). Each point on the line indicates the system's target value at $\mathcal{ES}$ - $\gamma_A^*, \gamma_B^*$, and $\gamma_C^*$, respectively [* for equilibrium].
abstract: We introduce Equilibrium State Estimation (ESE), a novel paradigm for simultaneous prediction, where multiple interacting systems require separate yet coordinated forecasts. Such scenarios often arise in real-world settings such as economics and healthcare modeling. Unlike existing approaches that predict one system at a time, ESE forecasts all systems in a single pass. It first estimates the equilibrium state across systems, then generates holistic forecasts based on the difference between the current state and the estimated equilibrium. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, including currency exchange and COVID-19 spread modeling, demonstrate that ESE is at least as accurate as state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods while being significantly faster. In addition, ESE integrates seamlessly with conventional predictors, combining their accuracy with its exceptional efficiency and delivering a 10-70x speedup. With linear-time complexity, ESE scales far better than SOTA methods as the number of systems increases. Moreover, it remains accurate under diverse perturbations, establishing ESE as a fast, generalizable, robust, and scalable multi-prediction method.
